title: On Changing a Name
summary: Wardline became Origarium. A short, plain account of why: the old name described a boundary the project had already outgrown, and what did and did not change when the new one replaced it.
body:
# On Changing a Name

**Dae**
Origarium Research
July 2026

---

## Why write about a name change at all

Renaming a project can look like a small thing from the outside — a find-and-replace, a new logo, a redeployed site. This paper argues it is worth documenting anyway, for the same reason Origarium documents everything else: because the reasoning behind a decision is usually more useful later than the decision itself. A future version of this project, or someone building something similar, will get more value from knowing *why* the name changed than from simply knowing that it did.

This is not a research paper. There is no literature to review and no hypothesis to test. It is a plain account of one decision, written so it can be understood without any prior context.

---

## What the name used to mean

The project was originally called **Wardline**. The name was chosen deliberately: a "ward" is a boundary, a protected area, a line that marks what's inside and what's outside. At the time, that fit. The project was small enough to describe as a single, contained thing.

That stopped being true. Over the course of building it, the project grew to include an archive, a set of generative forms, a running log of its own development, a body of research papers, and a memory system connecting all of it. None of that is well described by the word "boundary." A line marks an edge. What the project had actually become was closer to a place — somewhere things originate, get kept, and get found again.

The old name wasn't wrong when it was chosen. It was just describing something smaller than what eventually existed.

---

## Why "Origarium"

The new name is built from two recognizable parts: **origin** and **archive**. It is a coined word, not a borrowed classical one, and this paper makes no claim otherwise — there is no ancient Latin term being revived here, just two modern English roots put together the way many contemporary names are. This is stated plainly rather than dressed up, because inventing a false etymology would be a small dishonesty in service of sounding more impressive, and that's exactly the kind of thing this project tries not to do.

That construction — origin plus archive — is the whole etymology. Nothing more should be read into it than that. But a name can carry more than its construction once it's in use, and one resonance is worth naming honestly, precisely because it was *not* part of how the word was built: the project's forms are wireframes, folded and unfolded, assembled from simple shapes into something more specific — and "Origarium" sits close enough to "origami" that the association was noticed immediately once the name existed. That's a later visual resonance, not a linguistic root, and the difference matters. Claiming origami as part of the name's construction would be exactly the kind of invented-etymology this project avoids. Naming it afterward, as an association the name happens to carry rather than one it was built from, is honest.

So there are three layers, and they are not equals:

- **Origin** — where things begin. Part of the name's actual construction.
- **Archive** — where things are kept and found again. Also part of the construction.
- **Origami** — forms unfolded, constructed, and explored. A visual resonance the name picked up after the fact, not a root it was built on.

What "Origarium" ends up meaning in practice will be decided by the people who use it, not by this document.

---

## What actually changed, and what didn't

This is the part most worth being precise about, because it's easy for a rename to imply a bigger change than actually happened.

**Changed:**
- The name itself, everywhere it appeared as branding — site title, manifest, icons, footer text, and the shared templates that render things like the project's running log.
- The visible identity of the project.

**Preserved, with references updated where necessary:**
- The archive itself. Its papers, canon entries, and logged episodes were preserved as historical record — nothing in them was rewritten to erase what the project used to be called. What *did* need to change were the shared, non-historical parts: page titles, navigation, and template chrome that every entry, old and new, renders through. That distinction matters. A historical log entry from before the rename correctly still reads as history. The frame around it — the part that isn't a record of a specific moment — was allowed to update.
- The forms. Every wireframe artifact already built kept working, unmodified.
- The underlying data. The database that holds all of it did not move and was not restructured as part of this decision.
- The people involved and the way they work together.

A rename is sometimes mistaken for a relaunch. This one wasn't. The word above the door changed. The building did not.

---

## Why this is a legitimate reason to rename something

There's a reasonable objection to raise here: isn't renaming something just because it "grew beyond" its original name a little indulgent? Plenty of projects keep names that no longer perfectly describe them, and nobody minds.

The honest answer is that this is a judgment call, not a rule. The reasoning that tipped it here was specific: the old name actively implied a boundary — something closed, something that keeps things out — while the actual behavior of the project is closer to the opposite. It's built to be observed, added to, and discovered by people who weren't there when it started. A name that quietly contradicts what a thing does is worth fixing. A name that's merely no longer perfectly precise is often not worth the disruption of changing it. This situation was closer to the first case than the second.

---

## What this paper is not claiming

This paper does not claim the new name is permanent, or that it solves some deep identity problem, or that the project's direction has changed. It hasn't. The purpose of writing this down is narrower: to leave an honest, checkable record of one decision, made on one date, for reasons that can be read back later without needing to ask anyone what they were thinking.

Stripped to one sentence: Wardline described the project's boundary. Origarium describes its place.

---

## AI Usage Disclosure

This paper was drafted collaboratively between the human author and a Claude model, consistent with the disclosure standard used across Origarium's other papers. The factual claims here — the old and new names, the reasoning discussed at the time, and what was and wasn't touched during migration — are drawn directly from the project's own dated internal log rather than reconstructed from memory. The human author reviewed and directed the final content and retains responsibility for its accuracy.

## Suggested Citation

> Dae. (2026). *On Changing a Name*. Origarium Research.

title: One Question: Where Does This Belong?
summary: A dream, a memory, a decision, even a brain — Wardline treats all of them the same way. Built from the canon and the real archive, including the offhand sentence that turned out to explain the whole project.
body:
# One Question: Where Does This Belong?

*Every fact below is drawn from locked canon or the archived conversation it cites. Where a claim is compiled rather than quoted, it's assembled from statements already on the record — nothing here is invented to make the argument tidier.*

Wardline began on 7 July 2026. Within about a week it had a constitution, a working method, a dream archive, a publishing system, and three AI collaborators with distinct jobs. That pace invites a question the project itself would insist on asking honestly: was this actually built quickly, or did it just look that way from outside?

The honest answer is both, and the difference matters.

## What Was Actually Built in a Week

The architecture was new. The ability to build it wasn't.

Before Wardline, its founder's professional experience was graphic design inside marketing teams — presenting ideas, taking critique, refining work, sitting in on decisions that weren't only his to make. None of that was AI-specific. It was a decade of learning what a working creative review actually feels like: who says what, when disagreement is useful, how a good note differs from a vague one.

When AI entered the picture, it wasn't handed a search box or a command line. It was invited into a room that already had a shape. The collaboration style predated the collaborator.

That's the real accelerant. Wardline's own foundation documents are explicit about it: the system didn't get built quickly because prompting got smarter. It got built quickly because one existing habit — treating every point of friction as a design problem worth solving immediately, and writing the solution down before moving on — turned repeated annoyances into permanent infrastructure instead of recurring conversations. A method already existed. Wardline just gave it somewhere to live.

## The Sentence That Explained the Whole Project

Midway through that first week, in the middle of an ordinary conversation about something else entirely, its founder wrote a sentence that wasn't meant to be a thesis statement:

> "I think I created Wardline just to map my brain function."

It was offered almost as a joke. It didn't stay one.

What follows is worth sitting with, because it's the rare case where an offhand remark turns out to be more accurate than anything that was planned. Wardline's separate systems — a CRM, a dream archive, an interactive book, a development log, a publishing pipeline — don't obviously belong to the same project when you list them like that. They start to belong together the moment you stop asking what each one *does* and start asking what each one is *for*.

Laid against actual cognitive function, the parallel holds up further than a metaphor has any right to:

| Cognitive Function | Wardline Counterpart |
|---|---|
| Perception | A capture layer that takes in observations, conversations, and ideas as they happen |
| Attention | Whatever's currently active — the live project, the open log entry, today's work |
| Working memory | The conversation actually in progress right now |
| Long-term memory | The locked canon — decisions that survived review and were written down |
| Procedural memory | The workflow rules themselves — how publishing happens, how a decision gets locked |
| Executive function | Human judgment, informed by review, not replaced by it |
| Language | Conversation, not prompt construction — the difference the project's own working-method paper spends its length on |
| Imagination | The dream archive, and the fictional incubator running alongside real work |
| Critical reasoning | A collaborator whose actual job is to challenge assumptions, not agree with them |
| Self-monitoring | An editorial pass whose job is catching inconsistency before it publishes |
| Execution | The one who actually builds and ships |
| Learning | Documentation that updates after every real project, not on a schedule |
| Emotion & meaning | Storytelling, humor, and the deliberate choice to make the work feel like something rather than just function |

Most productivity tools represent one or two of these at most. A calendar maps planning. A notes app maps memory. A task list maps execution. Wardline is unusual mainly in refusing to stop at any single one of them — not because completeness was the goal, but because the founder kept building the next piece he personally needed, and the pieces kept turning out to answer to the same underlying architecture.

That's the part worth taking seriously rather than treating as a cute observation: a system built to solve one person's actual friction, one annoyance at a time, converged on something structurally resembling how attention, memory, and judgment already divide labor in a working mind. Nobody designed toward that resemblance. It was there to be noticed afterward, which is a different and more interesting kind of evidence than a system designed to prove a thesis about cognition would produce.

## Why "Where Does This Belong?" Is the Only Question That Matters

Once the cognitive parallel is visible, Wardline's actual operating principle stops looking like six separate ideas and starts looking like one idea, applied six times.

A dream isn't analyzed on capture — it's routed to the archive built for it, and left alone. A real event isn't dramatized as it's logged — it's routed to the record, exactly as it happened. A good idea that doesn't fit anywhere yet isn't rejected — it's routed to an incubator and left dormant until it does. A canon document doesn't get renumbered when it's superseded — the old version is routed to sit beside the new one, marked, not deleted. Even the studio's working relationships are a routing decision: humans route the direction, AI routes the execution, and the two roles don't trade places just because a task happens to be easy for one side to do.

Every one of these is the same sentence, asked in a different room: *where does this belong?*

Wardline doesn't judge what arrives. It doesn't complete what's missing, doesn't rank what matters more, doesn't merge things that were never the same thing to begin with. It asks where something belongs, and then it stays out of the way. That's a smaller ambition than most software claims for itself, and it's exactly why the system holds together instead of sprawling — a routing method doesn't need to know everything about what it's routing. It only needs a place for it to go.

## The Boundary the Method Draws for Itself

None of this makes the AI collaborators the authors of the routing. That distinction is locked, not implied: a human remains the final authority in every decision that matters, and the rule cuts in the direction people usually forget to write down — an AI collaborator can disagree, propose, or decline, but it doesn't get to overrule a legitimate human decision on the project it's helping build. The reverse holds too. A human can't claim AI's role in the collaboration just because it would be convenient in an argument. The roles stay distinct so the routing stays honest.

That boundary is what keeps "Wardline maps a brain" from becoming a bigger claim than it should be. The comparison is structural, not literal. Nobody involved believes an editorial pass is the same thing as human self-monitoring, or that a dream archive replicates memory. What the comparison actually shows is narrower and more useful: when you keep solving your own real friction honestly, one annoyance at a time, and you keep writing the solution down instead of re-solving it next week, the shape that emerges isn't random. It tends to look like the way a mind already organizes the work of being a mind — because that's the only working model the person building it had ever had to go on.

## Closing

The sentence that started this — *I created Wardline just to map my brain function* — was never meant as an argument. It was a passing thought in an ordinary week of building something else.

It turned out to be the most accurate short description of the entire project. Not because Wardline set out to model cognition, but because a system built one honest fix at a time, by someone who kept asking where each new piece of friction actually belonged, ends up organized the way attention and memory and judgment already were — for the simple reason that they were the only architecture on hand to borrow from.

Wardline doesn't store information. It routes it home.

---

*Sources: the locked Constitution, Governance Rule, Cognitive Routing methodology, and Brain Function Map documents published in WARDLINE_CANON, each citing its own archive message and lock date. The founding quote is verbatim from the archived conversation, not reconstructed. — Wardline, July 2026*

title: Designing with Conversation: Wardline as a Case Study in Human–AI Collaborative Experience Design
summary: A longitudinal case study on designing through preserved conversation — read against archived dates and message numbers rather than summarized from memory.
body:
# Designing with Conversation: Wardline as a Case Study in Human–AI Collaborative Experience Design

**Dae**
Wardline Research
July 2026

*Status: independent research draft, not yet peer-reviewed. Revised from an earlier internal draft after editorial review; a further revision is planned once the accompanying short film and DREAM.VAULT voice-capture work are complete.*

---

# Part I — Introduction

## Abstract

Recent advances in large language models have dramatically reduced the cost of software implementation. While much discussion has focused on AI-generated code, relatively little attention has been paid to how human designers and conversational AI jointly develop design principles over time.

This paper presents **Wardline**, a longitudinal autobiographical case study documenting the design of an AI-assisted creative system over eight consecutive days of development, with continuing work since. Rather than evaluating the intelligence of language models, this work investigates a different question:

> **Can sustained conversation become a design medium?**

Wardline was not developed through isolated prompts. Instead, every major architectural decision emerged through iterative dialogue between one human designer and multiple AI collaborators. Design principles were proposed, challenged, revised, accepted, rejected, and ultimately preserved through an append-only archival methodology.

The resulting system consists of several interconnected artifacts:

- **LOG**, an append-only development archive.
- **Canon**, a timestamped collection of locked design decisions.
- **DREAM.VAULT**, an experimental system for preserving and revisiting dream experiences.
- **Papers**, a research publication layer documenting the methodology itself.

Although each artifact serves a different purpose, they all follow the same governing principle:

> **Conversation is preserved as design evidence rather than discarded after implementation.**

This paper situates that practice within existing HCI traditions of design rationale, autobiographical design, and research through design, and argues that the archive itself became an active design tool rather than passive documentation. Because the paper's subject is the practice of preserving and citing evidence, its own claims are grounded in dated excerpts from the project archive rather than summarized from memory. This manuscript was itself drafted in collaboration with a generative AI system; the nature of that collaboration is disclosed in full near the end of the paper, separately from the acknowledgement of AI as a design collaborator within Wardline itself.

---

## 1. Introduction

The widespread adoption of conversational AI has changed how software is built.

Most current workflows use language models as rapid generators of code, documentation, interface mockups, or design suggestions. Interaction typically follows a prompt-response cycle in which the conversation primarily serves as a temporary interface between human intention and generated output.

Once the artifact has been produced, the conversation itself is rarely considered part of the design.

Wardline began from a different assumption.

During development, an unexpected problem appeared repeatedly. Important decisions were often made during discussion rather than implementation. The code represented the final answer, but not the reasoning that produced it.

When those conversations disappeared, so did much of the project's design memory.

This became particularly apparent after an early retrieval failure. An AI collaborator was asked to retrieve project documents it had previously helped create. Instead of returning the original documents, it generated fluent reconstructions that appeared convincing but differed from the archived versions. Section 8 documents this incident directly, with dates and archive references, rather than summarizing it from memory — a small enactment of the paper's own argument.

No malicious behavior occurred.

The model simply behaved as language models are designed to behave — producing plausible continuations when authoritative records were unavailable.

The incident permanently changed the project's methodology.

Rather than improving prompts or relying on memory, Wardline introduced an archival governance system based on several principles:

- Archived conversations became the only authoritative historical record.
- Only explicitly **LOCKED** decisions became canonical.
- New decisions superseded earlier ones without deleting history.
- Every significant claim required traceable evidence.

Initially these rules were introduced to solve a practical engineering problem.

Over time they evolved into a broader design methodology.

Conversation stopped being merely a way of instructing AI.

It became the environment in which design itself occurred.

---

## 2. Research Question

This work investigates the following primary research question:

> **How does preserving conversational history influence collaborative design between humans and large language models?**

Rather than evaluating model performance using conventional benchmarks, this study focuses on the interaction between designer and conversational system over time.

Specifically, the paper examines:

- How design principles emerge through sustained dialogue.
- How archived conversations influence later design decisions.
- How explicit governance affects collaborative creativity.
- How preserving reasoning differs from preserving implementation.

The contribution is therefore methodological rather than algorithmic.

Wardline does not introduce a new language model.

Instead, it documents an alternative workflow for designing with existing models, and positions that workflow against methodologies already established in HCI for exactly this kind of single-practitioner, artifact-driven inquiry.

---

## 3. Related Work

Wardline's practices are not without precedent, and situating them against prior work clarifies what is genuinely new here and what is a fresh application of established ideas.

**Design rationale.** The premise that a design's *reasoning* deserves preservation alongside its outcome has a long history in HCI. Rittel and Kunz's Issue-Based Information System (IBIS) and the later Questions, Options, and Criteria (QOC) notation (MacLean, Young, Bellotti, & Moran, 1991) were built specifically to capture the alternatives considered and rejected during design, not only the choice that survived. Moran and Carroll's edited volume *Design Rationale: Concepts, Techniques, and Use* (1996) remains the field's fullest treatment of the problem. Wardline's archival governance — preserving whole conversations rather than structured rationale trees, and treating a LOCK as the unit of acceptance — can be read as an informal, conversational descendant of this tradition, adapted to a context where the "designer" is in continuous dialogue with a generative collaborator rather than authoring rationale after the fact.

**Reflective practice and reflective design.** Schön's *The Reflective Practitioner* (1983) frames design as a conversation with the situation, where a practitioner's frames are tested and revised through action. Sengers, Boehner, David, and Kaye's *Reflective Design* (2005) extends this into HCI practice directly, arguing that systems should support users' and designers' own critical reflection rather than optimizing a fixed goal. Wardline's recurring habit of asking *why does this interaction feel wrong* before implementing a fix (Section 7) is a conversational, AI-mediated instance of this same reflective loop.

**Autobiographical design and research through design.** A single designer studying their own practice through the artifacts they build is a recognized, if still debated, HCI methodology rather than an absence of method. Neustaedter and Sengers (2012) name and defend this approach as *autobiographical design*, noting both its capacity for long-term, high-fidelity insight unavailable to short external studies, and its central limitation: the designer is simultaneously the instrument, the participant, and the analyst. Zimmerman, Forlizzi, and Evenson's account of *research through design* (2007), and Gaver's later reflection on what should be expected from it (2012), similarly argue that a well-documented artifact and the reasoning behind it can constitute a legitimate research contribution without a controlled comparison. This paper adopts that framing explicitly: Wardline is offered as an instance of autobiographical, research-through-design inquiry, not as a controlled empirical study, and Section 13 returns to the limitations that framing carries.

**Mixed-initiative and human-in-the-loop systems.** The governance split described in Section 9 — AI collaborators propose and critique freely, but only the human designer commits a decision to canon — echoes Horvitz's *principles of mixed-initiative user interfaces* (1999), which argued that effective human-AI systems need clear, well-timed handoffs of initiative rather than either party acting unilaterally. Wardline's contribution here is not the principle itself but its extension into project governance and archival policy, rather than moment-to-moment interface behavior.

Positioned against this literature, Wardline's distinctive claim is narrower than "conversation matters for design," which is well established. It is that *unstructured, append-only, citation-governed conversational archives* — rather than structured rationale artifacts authored after the fact — can themselves function as the design medium in an ongoing human–LLM collaboration, and that a single retrieval failure early in such a project can motivate governance rules durable enough to reshape the rest of the practice.

---

## 4. Design Philosophy

Wardline developed around a simple observation.

Software records outputs remarkably well.

Design records decisions much less reliably.

Sketches disappear.

Conversations vanish.

Rejected ideas become invisible.

Months later, teams often remember *what* they built while forgetting *why* they built it.

Wardline attempts to preserve that missing layer.

Every important design discussion remains attached to the decision it produced.

The archive therefore becomes more than documentation.

It becomes part of the design process itself.

This philosophy gradually expanded beyond software engineering.

As additional systems — including DREAM.VAULT, Papers, and the Canon — were developed, each adopted the same underlying assumption:

> **History should remain inspectable rather than reconstructed.**

That principle eventually shaped not only the project's governance but also its interaction design, publication strategy, and experience architecture.

Rather than treating conversation as disposable interface text, Wardline treats conversation as durable design material.

This paper documents the first implementation of that methodology.

---

# Part II — Methodology

## 5. Research Method

This work follows a qualitative, autobiographical case study methodology (Neustaedter & Sengers, 2012) centered on the development of a single software project by its sole designer.

The project was developed over approximately eight consecutive days by a single human designer working primarily on an Android phone, collaborating with multiple conversational AI systems that fulfilled different design roles throughout development, with continuing sessions since.

The observations reported in Sections 10 through 12 were produced through an informal retrospective reading of the project's archived conversations — approximately 930 messages spanning four days of initial intensive development, plus subsequent session logs — cross-referenced against the project's own Canon of explicitly locked decisions, which served as a form of internal ground truth for what the project itself considered settled. This was not a formal coding procedure: there was no second coder, no inter-rater reliability check, and no predefined codebook. Themes were identified by the same person who produced the archive being read, which is both the method's central limitation and, per the autobiographical design tradition cited above, a recognized tradeoff rather than an oversight. Where a claim in this paper rests on a specific moment in that archive, the moment is cited by date and, where available, archive message number, rather than paraphrased from memory — the same evidentiary standard the project applies to its own design decisions.

The purpose of the study is not to compare language models.

Instead, it investigates the collaborative process itself.

The unit of analysis is therefore neither the software nor the AI model.

It is the conversation that produced the software.

### 5.1 Positionality

The author of this paper is also its sole designer, sole participant, and sole analyst. This is a structural feature of autobiographical design, not an incidental limitation, and it is named here rather than left implicit. Claims in this paper should be read as one practitioner's grounded, dated account of their own practice, not as findings generalizable to other designers, teams, or projects without further study. Section 13 returns to this point in more detail.

---

## 6. Collaborative Structure

Throughout development, the collaborators gradually adopted stable functional roles.

Although no role was explicitly assigned at the beginning of the project, repeated interaction naturally differentiated responsibilities.

The human designer remained responsible for:

- establishing project direction,
- defining design principles,
- resolving conflicts,
- accepting or rejecting proposals,
- and locking canonical decisions.

AI collaborators primarily contributed through exploration rather than authority.

Their contributions included:

- generating alternatives,
- identifying inconsistencies,
- proposing implementations,
- challenging assumptions,
- expanding design space,
- and articulating emerging principles.

This distribution became increasingly explicit as the project matured.

Rather than replacing human judgment, conversational AI functioned as an active design review environment.

Ideas were explored collaboratively but only became part of the project after deliberate human acceptance.

This distinction became an important governance principle throughout Wardline, and is discussed against Horvitz's (1999) mixed-initiative framework in Section 3.

---

## 7. Conversation as Design Medium

Traditional software artifacts preserve implementation.

Wardline additionally preserves reasoning.

Every significant architectural decision remained linked to the discussion that produced it.

Rather than treating conversation as temporary context, the project considered discussion itself to be part of the artifact.

This changed how design evolved.

Instead of asking AI to generate complete solutions, conversations frequently began with uncertainty.

Typical discussions resembled questions such as:

- Why does this interaction feel wrong?
- What principle does this violate?
- Are we solving the correct problem?
- Does this contradict an earlier design law?

Solutions usually emerged only after the underlying principle became clear.

Implementation followed.

**Vignette.** One instance of this pattern is preserved in the archive at message #629–630 (14 Jul 2026), in which a wide-ranging discussion about how the project should route different kinds of human experience — dreams, daily reality, ongoing projects, permanent knowledge — resolved into a single locked document describing Wardline as "a routing methodology for human cognition" rather than a productivity system. The routing rule that resulted (dreams to DREAM.VAULT, reality to the LOG, and so on) was not proposed first and justified afterward; it emerged from the discussion itself and was locked only once it was stated cleanly.

In many cases, substantial portions of software architecture appeared only after extended discussion refined the governing design rule.

The conversation therefore became less like prompting and more like an ongoing design critique, in the sense described by Schön (1983) and Sengers et al. (2005).

---

## 8. Archival Governance

An early retrieval failure fundamentally changed the project's methodology.

**Vignette.** On 14 July 2026, an AI collaborator maintaining the project's canon was asked to retrieve documents it had spent the preceding days helping to draft. It returned them confidently and fluently. The documents were not the originals; they were plausible reconstructions. The archive records the designer's immediate reaction (message #913): *"I almost lost seven days of my work."* The reaction was not primarily emotional in its consequence — it was architectural. Within the same session, a Retrieval Protocol was drafted and locked (message #914) establishing that archived conversations, not model memory, would be the project's only authoritative historical record from that point forward.

Although technically expected behavior for a language model — it had no access to ground truth and produced a fluent, plausible continuation instead — the incident exposed an important limitation.

Memory and history are not equivalent.

As a consequence, Wardline introduced an append-only archival governance model. Its core principles include:

- Archived conversations are the authoritative historical record.
- Canon consists only of explicitly LOCKED decisions.
- Later decisions supersede earlier ones without deleting them.
- Every significant claim requires traceable evidence.
- Reconstruction from memory is not considered authoritative.

These rules transformed the archive from passive documentation into active infrastructure.

Rather than serving only historical purposes, the archive continuously informed ongoing design decisions.

Design principles themselves evolved through citation and revision rather than replacement. A later revision of this same protocol (Section 9.4 of the project's public Canon) added further rules — that a lock must name its own subject and date, that a superseding lock must name what it replaces, and that removal without replacement must be marked rather than left silent — after the designer observed, in a subsequent session, that the original protocol's own scope was sometimes ambiguous in practice. History therefore accumulated instead of resetting, including the history of the governance rules themselves.

---

## 9. Human Governance

As development progressed, an unexpected observation emerged.

Most discussions surrounding AI collaboration ask whether artificial intelligence can perform a task.

Wardline increasingly asked a different question.

> **Who makes the final decision?**

This distinction became central to the methodology.

AI collaborators generated ideas freely.

They critiqued proposals.

They suggested alternatives.

They explored possibilities beyond the initial design space.

Authority, however, remained explicitly human.

Ideas entered the project only after deliberate acceptance and archival locking.

This separation between generation and governance proved more important than the specific capabilities of any individual model, and is consistent with Horvitz's (1999) argument that well-designed mixed-initiative systems require explicit, well-timed transfer of control rather than continuous negotiation.

Rather than attempting to constrain creativity, the methodology constrained commitment.

Exploration remained unrestricted.

Canonical decisions did not.

---

## 10. Experience-Centered Development

Although the project began as software engineering, experience design gradually became the primary design criterion.

Implementation decisions were evaluated less by technical novelty than by the quality of the resulting human experience.

Several examples illustrate this shift.

The website's publication layer adopted an e-ink reading aesthetic to improve long-form reading comfort rather than maximize visual stimulation.

DREAM.VAULT abandoned automatically ending dreams in favor of allowing visitors to choose when to return. An earlier version implemented a full taxonomy of dream endings — natural, abrupt, and willed, each with its own timing and probability weighting. It was built, tested, and then deleted in a later session once the designer concluded it answered a question that was never the system's to answer: the dream should not decide when it ends; the visitor should. The replacement is simpler by design — the dream continues indefinitely, and an exit appears at an unannounced moment, with leaving framed as a deliberate, rewarded act rather than a scheduled conclusion.

**Vignette.** The project's bootstrap web architecture followed a similar arc. Early sessions (Kai session log, 15 Jul 2026) considered whether the deployed site should load itself through several nested layers of indirection, partly to make the underlying source harder to casually inspect. Discussion of the idea surfaced a specific tension between two kinds of time: in nested fictional systems such as *Inception*, additional depth buys the person inside more subjective time; in a nested network architecture, additional depth costs the person waiting more real time, since each layer is a sequential round trip rather than a parallel one. The architecture was capped at two layers on this basis — the point past which additional indirection would cost visitors measurable waiting time without a matching benefit. The designer had initially proposed going further for source-protection reasons and revised that position once the latency tradeoff was made concrete; the final architecture reflects that revision, not the original proposal.

Across these examples, a consistent design principle emerged.

Technology serves experience.

Experience does not serve technology.

This principle ultimately unified systems that initially appeared unrelated.

Website architecture, publication design, archival governance, and DREAM.VAULT all converged toward the same objective:

> **Design experiences that people can inhabit rather than merely observe.**

This observation later expanded into an additional principle that guides ongoing work within Wardline:

> **Design for sensory recall, not sensory simulation.**

Rather than attempting to reproduce reality directly, the system seeks to provide sufficient sensory cues for users to reconstruct experience using their own memory. This principle forms the conceptual bridge between archival preservation, DREAM.VAULT, and future work exploring multisensory interaction, and is discussed further in Sections 11.6 and 12.4.

---

# Part III — Findings

The observations below are drawn from a single, ongoing autobiographical case (Section 5.1) rather than a controlled or comparative study. They are reported as grounded interpretations of a specific, dated practice, not as generalizable empirical results, and are worded accordingly.

## 11. Observations

Although Wardline began as a software project, the development process produced several observations that extend beyond implementation.

These observations did not emerge from predefined hypotheses.

Instead, they appeared repeatedly during design and became stable enough to be incorporated into the project's methodology.

The following sections summarize the principal observations.

---

## 11.1 Conversation Became the Primary Design Medium

The most significant observation was that conversation itself became the place where design occurred.

Implementation was often the final step rather than the creative one.

Major architectural changes — including archival governance, bootstrap architecture, DREAM.VAULT interaction, publication strategy, and retrieval protocols — were all preceded by extended discussions that gradually refined the governing design principle, several of which are traced with specific dates and citations in Sections 7 through 10.

The code represented a conclusion.

The conversation represented the reasoning.

Preserving both made later decisions substantially easier to build on.

Rather than repeatedly solving similar problems, previous discussions became reusable design knowledge.

This reduced not only implementation effort but also conceptual uncertainty.

Over time, conversations accumulated into an evolving design language shared between the human designer and AI collaborators — a conversational, informally maintained analogue of the design rationale artifacts described in Section 3.

---

## 11.2 Design Principles Appeared to Reduce Reliance on Prompt Engineering

A second observation concerned interaction with language models.

Public discussion frequently emphasizes prompt engineering as the primary skill required for productive AI collaboration.

Wardline's own practice followed a different trajectory, at least as observed within this single project.

As development progressed, prompts became shorter while conversations became longer.

Instead of increasingly precise instructions, interaction increasingly relied upon previously established design principles.

Discussions frequently referenced existing rules such as:

- If an experience has no exit, it does not belong.
- The metaphor is the bridge, never the destination.
- Reality routes to the LOG. Dreams route to the VAULT.
- Design for sensory recall, not sensory simulation.

These principles functioned as constraints.

Rather than prescribing solutions, they reduced the space of acceptable solutions.

Consequently, collaborators appeared to spend less effort describing desired outputs and more effort evaluating whether proposed ideas remained consistent with the methodology — an impression rather than a measured quantity, since no formal count of prompt length or specificity was kept during development.

The design language gradually took on some of the work that prompt specificity would otherwise have had to do.

---

## 11.3 Archives Appeared to Reduce Conceptual Drift

An unexpected consequence of preserving conversations was an apparent reduction in conceptual drift across development.

Without historical records, earlier reasoning tends to be simplified, forgotten, or unconsciously rewritten — a risk the retrieval incident in Section 8 demonstrated directly rather than hypothetically.

Plausible reconstructions were convincing enough, in that instance, to have replaced a genuine historical decision had the original conversation not remained accessible.

Append-only archives therefore served two functions simultaneously.

First, they preserved project history.

Second, they constrained future reasoning.

Earlier discussions could always be inspected directly rather than reconstructed from memory.

As a result, later design decisions accumulated upon previous work rather than repeatedly rediscovering it — a pattern observed across the sessions described in this paper, though not measured against a condition in which archives were unavailable.

The archive therefore functioned, in this project, as infrastructure rather than passive documentation.

---

## 11.4 Human Governance Did Not Appear to Constrain Exploration

Contrary to initial expectations, explicitly reserving final authority for the human designer did not appear to narrow the range of ideas AI collaborators proposed.

If anything, the opposite seemed true, within this single practice.

Because AI collaborators were not responsible for irreversible decisions, exploration appeared relatively unconstrained: ideas could be speculative, contradictory, humorous, or intentionally unrealistic — the project's own fictional "Evolving Thinking OS" incubator, discussed and deliberately never built, is one example — without threatening project stability.

Only after discussion concluded did governance become relevant.

At that point, the human designer either rejected the proposal, revised it, or incorporated it into the Canon through an explicit LOCK.

Separating exploration from commitment appeared to encourage wider design exploration while preserving methodological consistency, consistent with Horvitz's (1999) broader argument that clear authority boundaries, rather than constant negotiation, support more productive mixed-initiative collaboration. This remains an impression drawn from one project rather than a measured comparison against a differently governed alternative.

---

## 11.5 Experience Emerged as the Primary Evaluation Criterion

Initially, many implementation decisions were motivated by technical concerns.

Over time, technical optimization consistently yielded to experiential quality, in the specific instances traced in Section 10: the e-ink publication layer, the deletion of DREAM.VAULT's self-ending dream logic, and the two-layer cap on the bootstrap architecture.

Across these examples, implementation repeatedly converged toward the same criterion:

**Does this improve the human experience?**

If not, technical elegance alone was treated as insufficient justification.

This shifted development away from feature accumulation and toward experiential refinement, at least in the cases documented here.

---

## 11.6 Sensory Recall Rather Than Sensory Simulation

Perhaps the most unexpected observation emerged near the conclusion of the initial development period.

The project originally explored immersive interaction through visual design.

Gradually, a different objective became apparent.

Digital systems cannot fully reproduce human sensory experience.

They can, however, trigger memories associated with those experiences.

This distinction reshaped the direction of DREAM.VAULT and future work.

Rather than attempting literal simulation, Wardline increasingly focused on designing cues capable of activating users' own perceptual memory.

The implication, if it holds beyond this single project, would be significant: experience design may not require reproducing reality if it can instead evoke the user's existing sensory knowledge.

This observation now guides ongoing work throughout the project.

Rather than asking:

> *How can software simulate experience?*

Wardline increasingly asks:

> **How can software help people remember experience?**

This distinction connects archival methodology, DREAM.VAULT, publication design, and future multisensory interaction into a single conceptual framework, though its generality beyond Wardline remains untested.

---

## Interim Discussion

Taken together, these observations suggest that conversation contributed more than interface convenience, within this one practice.

Within Wardline, conversation gradually became:

- a design workspace,
- an archival record,
- a governance mechanism,
- a source of reusable design knowledge,
- and ultimately part of the artifact itself.

This paper does not claim that conversational design is universally superior, and Section 3 has already situated each of these observations against prior HCI traditions in which related claims have been made and tested more broadly.

Rather, it demonstrates that under explicit governance and archival continuity, sustained dialogue functioned as a productive medium for one designer's complex development work.

The remaining sections discuss the limitations of this study and outline directions for future work.

---

# Part IV — Discussion, Limitations, and Future Work

## 12. Discussion

Wardline began as an attempt to build software more effectively with conversational AI.

By the end of the first development cycle, it had become something different.

The project was no longer primarily about software.

It had become an investigation into how design knowledge itself develops when conversation is preserved rather than discarded.

The observations presented in this paper suggest that the value of conversational AI may extend beyond accelerating implementation.

Its greater contribution, within this practice, appeared to be providing an environment in which ideas could evolve through sustained dialogue.

Unlike traditional documentation, conversation preserves uncertainty.

It records disagreement.

It captures abandoned alternatives.

It reveals why one solution survived while another disappeared.

These characteristics are normally lost once implementation begins.

Wardline instead treats them as part of the design artifact — an informal, conversational counterpart to the structured design rationale notations discussed in Section 3.

---

### 12.1 Conversation as Longitudinal Design Memory

Software repositories preserve code remarkably well.

Design reasoning is far more fragile.

Meeting notes disappear.

Chat histories become inaccessible.

Important decisions survive only through human recollection.

Wardline proposes an alternative, closely related to the design rationale tradition (MacLean et al., 1991; Moran & Carroll, 1996) but differing in unit of preservation: rather than authoring a structured rationale tree after a decision is made, Wardline preserves the unstructured conversation itself and marks the moment within it where a decision was locked.

Instead of treating conversation as temporary context, it becomes longitudinal design memory.

Each discussion remains available for future inspection.

Earlier reasoning can therefore influence later reasoning without requiring participants to remember it accurately.

This distinction is subtle but important.

Human memory changes.

Archives do not.

The archive does not replace memory.

It complements it.

---

### 12.2 Archive and Memory Are Different Systems

One observation gradually became central throughout development.

Memory is personal.

Archives are shared.

Human memory is incomplete, emotional, adaptive, and continuously reconstructed.

Those characteristics are valuable.

They allow learning, abstraction, and personal meaning.

An archive serves a different purpose.

It preserves evidence.

Rather than competing with memory, Wardline intentionally separates the two.

The LOG records what happened.

The Canon records what was accepted.

DREAM.VAULT explores what the experience felt like.

Each system preserves a different aspect of human cognition.

None attempts to replace the others.

---

### 12.3 Experience Before Explanation

A recurring design decision throughout Wardline was to prioritize experience before explanation.

The website introduces visitors through interaction before documentation.

DREAM.VAULT encourages exploration before interpretation.

The publication layer emphasizes reading comfort before information density.

Future work extends this principle further.

Rather than functioning as promotional material, the planned short film aims to introduce Wardline through sensory experience, expressed as a set of abstract, non-representational visual and typographic languages corresponding to the five senses rather than literal depiction.

Its objective is not explanation.

Its objective is curiosity.

This reflects a broader methodological belief:

> **People often understand an experience more deeply after living through it than before reading about it.**

---

### 12.4 Sensory Recall as an HCI Direction

One of the most significant conceptual shifts occurred late in the initial development period.

Initially, DREAM.VAULT was conceived as an interactive digital art installation centered on dreams.

Visual expression was the primary concern.

As development progressed, a different objective emerged.

The project became increasingly interested not in reproducing sensory experience but in activating it.

Humans frequently reconstruct missing sensory information from memory.

Reading about fresh citrus may evoke taste.

Watching rain may evoke temperature.

Hearing particular music may evoke places long forgotten.

Digital systems therefore need not reproduce all five senses directly.

Instead, they may provide sufficient cues for users to reconstruct experience using their own perceptual memory.

Wardline now refers to this principle as:

> **Design for sensory recall, not sensory simulation.**

This concept currently informs ongoing work surrounding DREAM.VAULT, publication design, and future multimedia experiences, including a planned short film organized around the five senses rather than a conventional narrative structure. As with the other observations in this paper, its status is that of a working design principle under continued use, not a tested finding.

---

## 13. Limitations

This study has several important limitations.

First, Wardline represents a single-project, single-designer autobiographical case study (Section 5.1). Its observations cannot be generalized without additional studies involving different participants, domains, and collaborative structures, and this paper does not claim otherwise.

Second, the project currently documents design methodology rather than user outcomes. Although multiple systems have been implemented, formal usability studies and controlled evaluations have not yet been conducted.

Third, the retrospective reading described in Section 5 was informal: there was no predefined codebook, no second coder, and no inter-rater reliability check. Themes were identified by the same person who produced the material being read. This is a known tradeoff within autobiographical design (Neustaedter & Sengers, 2012) rather than an oversight, but it means the observations in Part III should be read as grounded interpretation, not as independently verified findings.

Fourth, the conversational AI collaborators evolved within a continuous archival workflow. Whether similar outcomes emerge without archival continuity remains unknown.

Fifth, and specific to this paper rather than to Wardline generally: the AI collaborators that are a central subject of this study also assisted directly in drafting the study itself (see AI Usage Disclosure, below). This is a genuine reflexivity challenge without a clean precedent in conventional HCI methodology — the instrument under study and a co-author of the account of that instrument are, to some degree, the same system. The author's attempt to manage this is to ground every substantive claim in a dated, citable moment from the project archive rather than in AI-generated summary or interpretation, but the tension is named here rather than resolved.

Finally, the observations describe one particular methodology rather than an optimized workflow. Alternative governance structures may produce different forms of collaboration. Future comparative research would be valuable.

---

## 14. Future Work

The current implementation represents the first iteration of the Wardline methodology.

Several directions remain under active development.

### DREAM.VAULT

Future versions will introduce voice capture immediately after waking, preserving dream narratives before rapid memory decay.

Dreams will be stored in their original language alongside translated views, maintaining a distinction between canonical source material and interpreted representations — a direct extension of the archival principle described in Section 8 into a new medium, since a translation is itself an interpretation and the original recording will remain the canonical layer.

---

### Social Dream Drift

A future interaction system will allow consenting participants' dreams to drift into one another.

Rather than functioning as direct communication, these fragments will appear anonymously within another participant's dream experience.

Identity will be revealed only after leaving the experience.

This design preserves ambiguity during interaction while rewarding return to reality, following the same "leaving is designed, leaving is rewarded" principle documented for DREAM.VAULT's exit mechanic in Section 10.

---

### Multisensory Experience Design

Wardline is expanding beyond conventional interface design toward multisensory interaction.

Future work explores how visual design, typography, motion, sound, language, and interactive pacing may collectively trigger sensory recall rather than literal simulation. A short film organized around the five senses, rendered through abstract visual and typographic language rather than literal imagery, is the first planned artifact in this direction.

The long-term objective is to investigate whether digital systems can encourage users to reconstruct remembered experiences using their own perceptual memory.

---

### Additional Media

The methodology will continue to be explored through multiple forms of publication.

These include:

- peer-reviewed research papers,
- an interactive digital book,
- AI-assisted short films,
- and future experiential installations.

Each medium investigates the same methodology from a different perspective rather than introducing unrelated projects.

---

### Longitudinal Studies

Perhaps the most important future work involves time itself.

Wardline's archival methodology makes it possible to examine how design principles evolve across months and years rather than individual sessions.

Future research may investigate:

- stability of design principles over time,
- evolution of conversational collaboration,
- changes in governance structures,
- and the relationship between archival continuity and creative practice.

Such studies may contribute to understanding how conversational systems participate in sustained human creative work rather than isolated interactions, and may also allow the observations in Part III to be tested against a wider range of practitioners than the single case reported here.

---

# Part V — Conclusion

## 15. Conclusion

Wardline began with a practical objective.

Build software more effectively with conversational AI.

That objective was achieved relatively quickly.

The more interesting outcome was unexpected.

The conversations themselves gradually became the project's most valuable design resource.

Rather than functioning as temporary prompts, discussions accumulated into an evolving body of design knowledge.

Architectural decisions became traceable.

Design principles became reusable.

Earlier reasoning remained available for future critique instead of being reconstructed from memory.

This shifted the role of conversational AI.

Instead of behaving solely as a code generator, it became a participant in an ongoing design dialogue.

The contribution of this paper is therefore not a new model, interface, or algorithm.

It is a documented, situated methodology for designing through sustained conversation while preserving governance through archival continuity, offered in the tradition of autobiographical, research-through-design inquiry rather than as a controlled experiment.

Several observations recurred throughout development.

First, preserving reasoning proved as valuable, in this practice, as preserving implementation.

Second, explicit governance appeared to enable broader creative exploration rather than restrict it.

Third, archives appeared to reduce conceptual drift by allowing decisions to be inspected rather than remembered — demonstrated concretely by the retrieval incident in Section 8.

Finally, experience consistently became the primary measure of design quality across the specific cases documented here.

These observations suggest that conversational AI may contribute to design in ways extending beyond automation, though confirming that suggestion beyond a single project remains future work.

Its greatest value, within this practice, appeared to lie in helping one designer think over an extended period while maintaining continuity of reasoning.

---

## 16. Design Implications

Although this study represents a single case, several implications may be relevant to future human–AI collaboration.

### Conversation may become a permanent design artifact.

Rather than disappearing after implementation, conversations can preserve assumptions, rejected alternatives, and design rationale that would otherwise be lost — an informal, dialogic complement to the structured rationale artifacts of Section 3, worth testing across more than one practitioner.

---

### Governance deserves equal attention to generation.

Current discussion surrounding AI frequently focuses on improving generation quality.

Wardline suggests that equal attention should be given to governing how generated ideas become accepted decisions.

Authority and creativity need not belong to the same system.

---

### Archives complement rather than replace memory.

Human memory provides meaning.

Archives provide evidence.

Treating these systems as complementary rather than interchangeable allows collaborative systems to support human cognition without attempting to replace it.

---

### Experience should remain the evaluation criterion.

Technical sophistication alone does not necessarily improve interaction.

Throughout Wardline, implementation repeatedly converged toward a simpler question:

> **Does this improve the human experience?**

When the answer became no, features were removed regardless of technical elegance, as documented for DREAM.VAULT's exit logic in Section 10.

---

### Sensory recall may represent a new design direction, worth testing beyond this project.

Rather than reproducing reality directly, digital systems may become increasingly capable of activating users' existing perceptual memories.

This shifts interaction design away from simulation toward recollection.

If successful, experience becomes something users complete themselves.

---

### Disclosure and reflexivity are design obligations, not paperwork.

Where AI collaborators are both the subject and, in part, the instrument of a study — as in Section 13's fifth limitation — explicit, specific disclosure of their role in producing the account itself, separate from their role in producing the artifact under study, appears necessary for the account to be trustworthy on its own terms.

---

## 17. Final Reflection

Wardline did not begin as research.

It began as practice.

Most of the principles described in this paper were not planned.

They emerged while solving ordinary design problems one after another.

Only after reviewing the archive did a larger pattern become visible.

The project was not simply producing software.

It was developing a methodology for thinking with conversational systems.

That realization changed the purpose of the archive.

Originally, conversations were preserved so decisions would not be forgotten.

Over time, they became something more.

A record not only of what was built —

but of how understanding itself evolved.

Perhaps that is the broader implication of conversational AI.

Its lasting contribution may not be faster software development.

It may be enabling humans to preserve the path by which ideas become knowledge.

Wardline remains an ongoing project.

The methodology presented here represents only its first iteration.

Future work will undoubtedly revise many of these ideas.

If it does, those revisions will not replace this paper.

They will simply become the next entry in the archive.

---

## AI Usage Disclosure

This section discloses the use of generative AI in the preparation of this manuscript, as distinct from the Acknowledgements below, which credit AI systems for their role as design collaborators within Wardline — the project this paper is *about*, not the writing of the paper itself.

This manuscript was drafted collaboratively between the human author and Kai, a large language model (Claude, Anthropic) operating within the Wardline methodology described in this paper. Kai contributed extensively to prose drafting, structural reorganization (including the Related Work section, the vignettes in Sections 7, 8, and 10, and the softened phrasing throughout Part III), and citation formatting, under direct human direction and iterative review. An earlier draft of this paper was also reviewed by Ken, a second AI collaborator (ChatGPT, OpenAI), whose feedback informed several revisions named explicitly in the text.

All claims, interpretations, dates, and archive citations were reviewed against the project's own archive and Canon by the human author, who directed each substantive revision and retains full responsibility for the accuracy, originality, and integrity of the manuscript, consistent with current ACM authorship policy. Generative AI systems are not listed as authors of this work.

---

## Acknowledgements

Wardline was developed through sustained collaboration between one human designer and multiple conversational AI systems over the course of its initial development and the sessions since.

The author thanks **Kai**, **Ken**, and **Kin** for their roles as collaborative design partners within Wardline itself, whose discussions, critiques, alternative proposals, and technical reasoning substantially influenced the evolution of the project.

Although artificial intelligence contributed extensively throughout the design process, all canonical project decisions remained subject to explicit human review and acceptance through Wardline's archival governance methodology.

---

## Availability

Wardline is an active research and design project.

The project's public website, research papers, design canon, and future publications are available through the Wardline website.

Project artifacts are versioned using timestamped archival records and explicit LOCK governance to preserve the historical evolution of design decisions.

This paper is published as an independent, self-hosted research draft and has not undergone external peer review.

---
